newsitem.title: USA: Tobacco cos. say disclosure laws spreading.
newsitem.headline: Tobacco cos. say disclosure laws spreading.

text.p: More than a dozen states have legislation pending that is similar to a Massachusetts law requiring tobacco companies disclose each brands' ingredients, according to filings with a federal appeals court.

Lawyers for Philip Morris, R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co, Brown & Williamson Tobacco and Lorillard Tobacco said in papers filed with the U.S. 1st Circuit note that since the Massachusetts' law was signed last year similar measures have been "introduced in more than a dozen other states mandating disclosure of ingredient and nicotine-yield information," according to court papers.

The industry is calling upon the U.S. 1st Circuit Court of Appeals to overturn a lower court ruling on the Massachusetts law that requires companies to disclose each brands' ingredients by weight or measure to the state health department, which will then make the information available to the public.
The Massachusetts law is expected to go into effect Nov. 1.
Some 31 states and the city of San Francisco have filed friend-of-the-court briefs supporting Massachusetts in the case which will be argued on June 6.

The tobacco industry claims the Massachusetts' measure would have its "primary effects outside" the state particularly as Massachusetts officials have said they will publish the information on the Internet.
"Once the Commonwealth has disclosed the manufacturers' trade secrets, those trade secrets will have been destroyed forever," lawyers for the companies argued in their appeal.

Meanwhile the industry continued to hold talks with a core group of state attorneys general aimed at resolving state suits seeking to recoup Medicaid costs of smokers along with hundreds of individual and class action cases brought by smokers and their families.
It remained unclear on Thursday if any settlement from the talks would cover the issue of ingredient disclosure, said one official who asked not to be identified.
"It seems it would be in their interests, but I'm not sure if it is in the interests of the states," the official said.
